2024 in spaceflight  
|  |  
| --- |  
|  [Timeline of spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_spaceflight "Timeline of spaceflight") ← [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_spaceflight "2023 in spaceflight") [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_spaceflight "2025 in spaceflight") →  |  
2024 saw new world records for orbital launch attempts and successful orbital launches for the fourth consecutive year. Notable milestones included the successful maiden launches of the American [Vulcan Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcan_Centaur "Vulcan Centaur") and China's [Gravity-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity-1 "Gravity-1"), and [Long March 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_12 "Long March 12") rockets. The European [Ariane 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariane_6 "Ariane 6") rocket also conducted its inaugural flight, though it experienced a partial failure. [SpaceX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX") advanced its [Starship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Starship "SpaceX Starship") development, with [flight test 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starship_flight_test_5 "Starship flight test 5") achieving the first landing of its first stage. Additionally, the final launch of a [Delta family rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_\(rocket_family\) "Delta \(rocket family\)"), a [Delta IV Heavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_IV_Heavy "Delta IV Heavy") variant, occurred in April.
In September, the private [Polaris Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris_Dawn "Polaris Dawn") mission made history by performing the first commercial [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk"), during which two crew members exited their [Crew Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon "Crew Dragon") spacecraft. This mission set a new record for the number of individuals—four—simultaneously exposed to the vacuum of space.
Two significant scientific missions were launched in October: [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Europa Clipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_Clipper "Europa Clipper") to Jupiter's moon [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_\(moon\) "Europa \(moon\)") to look for signs of an ocean under its icy surface and [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency")'s [Hera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hera_\(space_mission\) "Hera \(space mission\)") to the [Didymos binary asteroid system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65803_Didymos "65803 Didymos") that was impacted four years earlier by the [DART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Asteroid_Redirection_Test "Double Asteroid Redirection Test") spacecraft to validate the [kinetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_energy "Kinetic energy") impact method of redirecting an asteroid on a trajectory to collide with Earth. On Mars, NASA's [Ingenuity helicopter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenuity_\(helicopter\) "Ingenuity \(helicopter\)") concluded operations in January after completing 72 flights when its rotor blades sustained critical damage.
The year also featured notable lunar missions. [CNSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_National_Space_Administration "China National Space Administration")'s [Chang'e 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'e_6 "Chang'e 6") successfully completed the first-ever sample return mission from [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"). [JAXA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA "JAXA")'s [SLIM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_Lander_for_Investigating_Moon "Smart Lander for Investigating Moon") and [Intuitive Machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitive_Machines "Intuitive Machines")' [IM-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IM-1 "IM-1") achieved soft landings on the lunar surface; however, both landers tipped over during their final descent, leading to the conclusion of their missions shortly thereafter. With SLIM, Japan became the fifth country to accomplish a soft landing on the Moon.
A record for the most people simultaneously in orbit was set on 11 September, with 19 individuals. This was achieved following the launch of the three-person [Soyuz MS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-26 "Soyuz MS-26") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS), joining the nine crew members already aboard the ISS, the three crew members of China's [Tiangong space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiangong_space_station "Tiangong space station"), and the four crew members of Polaris Dawn.
Throughout the year, the ISS hosted long-duration Expedition [70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_70 "Expedition 70"), [71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_71 "Expedition 71"), and [72](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_72 "Expedition 72") missions, as well as two short-term missions: the four-person crew of the privately operated [Axiom Mission 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_Mission_3 "Axiom Mission 3") (which included [Alper Gezeravcı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alper_Gezeravc%C4%B1 "Alper Gezeravcı"), the first [Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") astronaut) and the Russia's [21st Visiting Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_visiting_expeditions_to_the_International_Space_Station "List of visiting expeditions to the International Space Station") (which included [Maryna Vasileuskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryna_Vasileuskaya "Maryna Vasileuskaya"), the first [Belarusian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus") cosmonaut to reach space, excluding Soviet and Russian citizens of Belarusian origin). Meanwhile, Tiangong was visited by the long-term Shenzhou [18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhou_18 "Shenzhou 18") and [19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhou_19 "Shenzhou 19") missions.
## Overview
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]
### Astronomy and astrophysics
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Astronomy and astrophysics")]
On [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") at 3:40 UTC marking the first launch of the new year, [ISRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISRO "ISRO") launched their [XPoSat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPoSat "XPoSat") for studying [X-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") [polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarization_\(waves\) "Polarization \(waves\)"). It will serve as a complement to the present [IXPE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IXPE "IXPE") probe of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-4) Later the [ISRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISRO "ISRO")'s [Aditya-L1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aditya-L1 "Aditya-L1") spacecraft launched 5 months previously was inserted into a [halo orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_orbit "Halo orbit") around the Earth-Sun [L1 point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L1_point "L1 point") on 6 January. It will study the solar atmosphere, solar magnetic storms, and their impact on the environment around Earth.
[Einstein Probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_Probe "Einstein Probe"), [X-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") [space telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_telescope "Space telescope") mission by the [Chinese Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Academy_of_Sciences "Chinese Academy of Sciences") (CAS) in partnership with [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA "ESA") and the [Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck_Institute_for_Extraterrestrial_Physics "Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics") (MPE) dedicated to time-domain [high-energy astrophysics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-energy_astrophysics "High-energy astrophysics"), was launched on 9 January 2024.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-5)
In April 2024, NASA began, under the direction of the [Office of Science and Technology Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Science_and_Technology_Policy "Office of Science and Technology Policy") to create a standard for time on the Moon, it is called [Coordinated Lunar Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Lunar_Time "Coordinated Lunar Time") and is expected to be completed by 2026.
The [Space Variable Objects Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Variable_Objects_Monitor "Space Variable Objects Monitor") (SVOM) is a small [X-ray telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_telescope "X-ray telescope") satellite for studying the explosions of massive stars by analyzing the resulting [gamma-ray bursts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma-ray_burst "Gamma-ray burst"), developed by [China National Space Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_National_Space_Administration "China National Space Administration") (CNSA), [Chinese Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Academy_of_Sciences "Chinese Academy of Sciences") (CAS) and the French Space Agency ([CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES")),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-Leicester-6) launched on 22 June 2024 (07:00:00 UTC).
[European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") launched their [PROBA-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PROBA-3 "PROBA-3") dual satellites for solar [coronagraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronagraph "Coronagraph") on 5 December 2024 on a [PSLV-XL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSLV-XL "PSLV-XL") rocket.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-7)
### Exploration of the Solar System
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exploration of the Solar System")]
NASA's Mars helicopter _[Ingenuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenuity_\(helicopter\) "Ingenuity \(helicopter\)")_ flew its 72nd and last flight on 18 January. Because all four of its rotor blades were damaged, NASA subsequently announced the end of mission for Ingenuity on 25 January.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-NASA_20240125-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-9)
On 7 October, the ESA [_Hera_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hera_\(space_mission\) "Hera \(space mission\)") spacecraft was launched successfully. It will arrive at the asteroid [Didymos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didymos_\(asteroid\) "Didymos \(asteroid\)") in 2026 after [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") flyby, where it will study the effects of the [Double Asteroid Redirection Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Asteroid_Redirection_Test "Double Asteroid Redirection Test").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-10)
NASA's [Europa Clipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_Clipper "Europa Clipper") mission launched on 14 October to study the Galilean moon [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_\(moon\) "Europa \(moon\)") while in orbit around [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-11)
### Lunar exploration
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Lunar exploration")]
#### Artemis Program
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Artemis Program")]
In November, stacking operation begun for the [Artemis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_II "Artemis II") SLS solid rocket boosters segments.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-12) On 5 December, NASA updated the mission timeline, where [Artemis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_II "Artemis II") was delayed from 2025 September to 2026 April, and [Artemis III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_III "Artemis III") from 2026 September to mid-2027. The delay is mainly attributed to problems involving the heat shield of the Orion spacecraft.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-15)
#### Peregrine
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Peregrine")]
[Peregrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peregrine_Mission_One "Peregrine Mission One") lunar lander was successfully launched on 8 January, but after the launch a propellant leak was detected that precluded any attempt to perform a lunar landing. In the end, the Peregrine spacecraft never left the (highly elliptical) Earth orbit it was injected into by the carrier rocket, and the mission ended ten days later (after one orbit) on 18 January when the spacecraft re-entered the Earth's atmosphere (under control of the mission team) and was destroyed.
#### SLIM
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: SLIM")]
[SLIM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_Lander_for_Investigating_Moon "Smart Lander for Investigating Moon") achieved the first-ever lunar soft landing for a Japanese spacecraft.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-16) It landed on 19 January 2024 at 15:20 UTC, making Japan the 5th country to soft land on the Moon.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-17) Although it landed successfully, it landed on its side with the solar panels oriented westwards facing opposite the Sun at the start of [lunar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_day "Lunar day"), thereby failing to generate enough power.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-18) The lander operated on an internal battery power, which was fully drained that day.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-:8-19)
Irrespective of this solar array issue on lander, the two LEV 1 and 2 rovers, deployed during hovering just before final landing worked as expected, with LEV-1 communicating independently to the ground stations.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-:8-19) LEV-1 conducted seven hops over 107 minutes on lunar surface. Images taken by LEV-2 show the wrong attitude landing with loss of an engine nozzle during descent and even possible sustained damage to lander's Earth bound antenna, that is not pointed towards Earth.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-youtube.com-20) Irrespective of wrong attitude and loss of communication with the lander, the mission was fully successful after confirmation of its primary goal landing within 100 m (330 ft) of its landing spot was already achieved.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-22)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-youtube.com-20)
On 29 January, the lander resumed operations after being shut down for a week. JAXA said it re-established contact with the lander and its solar cells were working again after a shift in lighting conditions allowed it to catch sunlight.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-23) After that, SLIM was put in sleep mode for impending harsh [lunar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_night "Lunar night"). While SLIM was expected to operate only for one lunar daylight period, or 14 Earth days, with its on-board electronics not designed to withstand the −120 °C (−184 °F) nighttime temperatures on the Moon, it managed to survive three lunar nights, waking up on 25 February, 27 March and 24 April respectively, sending back more data and images. This feat of surviving lunar night without a [radioisotope heater unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioisotope_heater_unit "Radioisotope heater unit") was only previously achieved by some landers in the [Surveyor program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_program "Surveyor program").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-moneycontrol.com-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-27)
#### Nova-C
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Nova-C")]
[IM-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IM-1 "IM-1") [Nova-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova-C "Nova-C") Odysseus launched on 15 February 2024 towards the Moon via [Falcon 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9") on a direct intercept trajectory and later landed in the south polar region of the Moon on 22 February 2024 and became the first successful private lander and the first to do so using [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic "Cryogenic") [propellants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propellants "Propellants"). Though it landed successfully, one of the lander's legs broke upon landing and it tilted up on other side, 18° due to landing on a slope, but the lander survived and payloads were functioning as expected.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-28)
Just before landing, at approximately 30 m (98 ft) above the lunar surface, the _Odysseus_ lander was planned to eject the [EagleCam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EagleCam "EagleCam") camera-equipped [CubeSat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CubeSat "CubeSat"), which would have been dropped onto the lunar surface near the lander, with an impact velocity of about 10 m/s (22 mph). However, due to complications arising from the software patch, it was decided that EagleCam would not be ejected upon landing. It was later ejected on 28 February returning all types of data, except post IM-1 landing images that were the main aim of its mission.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-32)
The lander also includes the [Lunar Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arch_Mission_Foundation#Lunar_Library "Arch Mission Foundation") that contains a version of the [English Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Wikipedia "English Wikipedia"), artworks, selections from the [Internet Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Archive "Internet Archive"), portions of the [Project Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gutenberg "Project Gutenberg"), and more. It is projected to reside on the Moon in a readable state for billions of years.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-34)
#### China Lunar Exploration Program
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: China Lunar Exploration Program")]
Main article: [Chinese Lunar Exploration Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Lunar_Exploration_Program "Chinese Lunar Exploration Program")
On 13 March, China attempted to launch two spacecrafts, DRO-A and DRO-B, into [distant retrograde orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distant_retrograde_orbit "Distant retrograde orbit") around the Moon, but the mission failed to reach the strived for orbit, remaining stranded in a highly eliptical low Earth orbit.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-36) Tracking data appears to show China attempted to salvage the spacecraft and they appear to have succeeded in reaching their desired orbit.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-38)
On 20 March, China launched its relay satellite, [Queqiao-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queqiao-2 "Queqiao-2"), to lunar orbit, along with two mini satellites [Tiandu 1 and 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiandu "Tiandu"). Queqiao-2 will relay communications for the Chang'e 6 (far side of the Moon), Chang'e 7 and Chang'e 8 (Lunar south pole region) spacecrafts. Tiandu 1 and 2 will test technologies for a future lunar navigation and positioning constellation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-39) All the three probes entered lunar orbit successfully on 24 March 2024 (Both were attached to each other and separated in lunar orbit on 3 April 2024).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-41)
China sent [Chang'e 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'e_6 "Chang'e 6") on 3 May 2024, which conducted the first lunar sample return from [Apollo Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_\(crater\) "Apollo \(crater\)") on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-AJ_FI-20230425-42) This is China's second lunar sample return mission, the first was achieved by [Chang'e 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'e_5 "Chang'e 5") from the lunar near side four years earlier.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-43) It carries several international payloads as well as an un-(pre)announced Chinese mini-rover called _Jinchan_ to conduct [infrared spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absorption_spectroscopy "Absorption spectroscopy") of lunar surface and imaged Chang'e 6 lander on lunar surface.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-44) The lander-ascender-rover combination was separated from the orbiter and returner before landing on 1 June 2024 at 22:23 UTC. It landed on the Moon's surface on 1 June 2024.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-AJ_FI-20240601-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-segeryu240602-46) The ascender was launched back to lunar orbit on 3 June 2024 at 23:38 UTC, carrying samples collected by the lander, and completed rendezvous and docking with the waiting orbiter in lunar orbit. The sample container was transferred to the returner, which landed in [Inner Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Mongolia "Inner Mongolia") on 25 June 2024, completing China's lunar far side sample return mission. [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan") sent a lunar orbiter called [ICUBE-Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICUBE-Q "ICUBE-Q") along with Chang'e 6. The lander also placed a small national flag of China, made of [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt "Basalt"), a substance that occurs in vast quantities on the Moon's surface, to demonstrate the spirit of in situ resource utilization.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-47) After dropping off the return samples for Earth, the Chang'e 6 (CE-6) orbiter was successfully captured by the [Sun-Earth L2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun-Earth_L2 "Sun-Earth L2") Lagrange point on 9 September 2024.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-48)
#### Future
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Future")]
[DARPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA "DARPA") provided funding towards a forward looking 10 year lunar architecture proposals. Aimed at creating the beginning stages of a lunar economy the [DARPA lunar programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA_lunar_programs "DARPA lunar programs") is participated in by many current industry leaders.
### Human spaceflight
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Human spaceflight")]
On 4 February, Russian [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonaut "Cosmonaut") [Oleg Kononenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Kononenko "Oleg Kononenko") broke the world record for the most time spent in space, when he surpassed the previous record of 878 days, 11 hours, 29 minutes and 48 seconds held by retired cosmonaut [Gennady Padalka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gennady_Padalka "Gennady Padalka").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-49) After Kononenko returned on 23 September, the new records stands at 1110 days, 14 hours and 57 minutes.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-50)
On 5 June, [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing "Boeing")'s [Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") spacecraft conducted its [crewed test flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crewed_Flight_Test "Boeing Crewed Flight Test").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-51) [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams") became the first woman to fly on the maiden crewed flight of an orbital spacecraft (for a suborbital spacecraft, similar feat was accomplished by [Wally Funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Funk "Wally Funk") on [Blue Origin NS-16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin_NS-16 "Blue Origin NS-16") mission of [New Shepard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Shepard "New Shepard")).
On 11 September, following the launch of [Soyuz MS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-26 "Soyuz MS-26"), [a record breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_spaceflight_records#Human_spaceflight_firsts "List of spaceflight records") 19 people were simultaneously in orbit around Earth. In addition to the crew of MS-26, this included the crews of [Polaris Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris_Dawn "Polaris Dawn"), [Boe-CFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crew_Flight_Test "Boeing Crew Flight Test"), [SpaceX Crew-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-8 "SpaceX Crew-8"), [Soyuz MS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-25 "Soyuz MS-25") and [Shenzhou 18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhou_18 "Shenzhou 18").
On 17 December, two Chinese astronauts, [Cai Xuzhe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cai_Xuzhe "Cai Xuzhe") and [Song Lingdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_Lingdong "Song Lingdong"), completed the longest spacewalk in human history, of 9 hours and 6 minutes, with the assistance of the space station's robotic arms and ground-based scientific personnel, completed tasks such as the installation of space debris protection devices, inspection, and maintenance of external equipment and facilities.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-52)
#### Private human spaceflight and space tourism
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Private human spaceflight and space tourism")]
[SpaceX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX") launched [Axiom Mission 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_Mission_3 "Axiom Mission 3") aboard a [Crew Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon "Crew Dragon") spacecraft on a [Falcon 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9 "Falcon 9") rocket to the International Space Station (ISS) on 18 January 2024. The successful mission ended with a splashdown on 9 February 2024.
On 26 January,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-53) [Virgin Galactic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Galactic "Virgin Galactic")'s [SpaceShipTwo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceShipTwo "SpaceShipTwo") [VSS _Unity_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSS_Unity "VSS Unity") was successfully launched from [Spaceport America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceport_America "Spaceport America") on [Galactic 06](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galactic_06 "Galactic 06") suborbital [space tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tourism "Space tourism") mission. [Galactic 07](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galactic_07 "Galactic 07") launched on 8 June, the final flight of _Unity_ suborbital spaceplane.
[Blue Origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin "Blue Origin")'s [New Shepard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Shepard "New Shepard") also returned to suborbital space tourism launches with the successful [NS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin_NS-25 "Blue Origin NS-25") mission on 19 May. The next mission, [NS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin_NS-26 "Blue Origin NS-26"), took place on 29 August and [NS-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin_NS-28 "Blue Origin NS-28"), that took place on 22 November.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-54)
[Polaris Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris_Dawn "Polaris Dawn"), featuring the first commercial [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk"), launched on 10 September 09:23 UTC. On 11 September, the spacecraft reached an altitude of 1400 km, which is farther from Earth than any person has been since [Apollo 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17 "Apollo 17").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-55)
### Rocket innovation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Rocket innovation")]
The maiden flight of [United Launch Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Launch_Alliance "United Launch Alliance")'s [Vulcan Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcan_Centaur "Vulcan Centaur") took place on 8 January 2024. Vulcan is the first methane fueled rocket to reach orbit on its first attempt, and the first methane fueled rocket to reach orbit from the US.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-56)
China's Orienspace's [Gravity-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity-1 "Gravity-1") rocket completed its successful maiden flight on 11 January 2024, debuting on a new mobile sea platform in the Yellow Sea while breaking records as both the world's largest solid-fuel carrier rocket and China's most powerful commercial launch vehicle to date (as of early 2024).
On 5 March, for the first time due to their fast turnaround of 1 hour 51 minutes between launches, SpaceX launch operations for a mission (in this case, [Starlink Group 6-41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starlink "Starlink")) coincided with that of a preceding launch (in this case, payload deployment of [_Transporter-10_ :(53 payloads SmallSat Rideshare)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_spaceflight_launches_in_January%E2%80%93June_2024#SpXTransporter10 "List of spaceflight launches in January–June 2024").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-57)
On 13 March, the [KAIROS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KAIROS_\(rocket\) "KAIROS \(rocket\)") rocket from [Space One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_One "Space One") company attempted its maiden flight. The rocket was destroyed in an explosion five seconds after lift-off. No injuries were caused by the explosion.
On 11 April, another test flight of the Russian [Angara A5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angara_A5 "Angara A5") launched, with the [Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blok_DM-03 "Blok DM-03") upper stage being used for the first time.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-59)
On 7 May, [Long March 6C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_6C "Long March 6C") flew its successful maiden mission.
[SpaceX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX")'s [Starship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Starship "SpaceX Starship") launched its fourth integrated flight test ([IFT-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Starship_integrated_flight_test_4 "SpaceX Starship integrated flight test 4")) on 6 June 2024. The launch resulted in the successful controlled splashdown of both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship vehicle.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-60)
In June, [Stoke Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Space "Stoke Space") tested its [full flow staged combustion cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_flow_staged_combustion_cycle "Full flow staged combustion cycle") (FFSC) engine with a successful hotfire, the test marks only the fourth FFSC engine to have made it far enough in development to reach hotfire.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-61)
The maiden launch of [Ariane 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariane_6 "Ariane 6") occurred on 9 July, but it was a partial failure as though CubeSats were deployed correctly, but the second stage failed to relight due to an anomaly with an [auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-63) The second stage could not be deorbited and payloads studying and testing re-entry could not be deployed.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-64)
On 13 October, [Starship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Starship "SpaceX Starship") flew its [fifth orbital flight test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starship_flight_test_5 "Starship flight test 5") during which, for the first time, the first stage booster was recovered. This makes [Super Heavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Super_Heavy "SpaceX Super Heavy") the second ever orbital class rocket booster to be recovered by the use of [retropropulsive landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrorocket#Reusable_launch_systems "Retrorocket") (first being the Falcon 9 booster). 
On 30 November, [Long March 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_12 "Long March 12") successfully launched on its debut flight. Importantly, the launch also marked the debut of the [YF-100K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YF-100#Versions "YF-100") engine that will power the first stage of [Long March 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_10 "Long March 10") which is expected to send Chinese astronauts to the Moon before 2030.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-65)
The maiden flight of [Blue Origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin "Blue Origin")'s [New Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Glenn "New Glenn") was planned for November.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-66) Initial rollout of the vehicle and testing was completed in February[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-67) and in May Blue Origin planned to conduct additional testing in preparation for launch.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-blueorigin-20240524-68) On 12 June Blue Origin received the communications license necessary for the flight.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-fccspace-20240612-69) The launch was rescheduled for December 2024 or early 2025.
### Satellite technology
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_spaceflight&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Satellite technology")]
[Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plankton,_Aerosol,_Cloud,_ocean_Ecosystem "Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem") or PACE, a NASA Earth-observing satellite, launched on 8 February 2024.
In March, China successfully launched the [Queqiao-2 relay satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queqiao-2_relay_satellite "Queqiao-2 relay satellite") mission. The satellite is designed to act as a communication relay between Chang’e missions (including the [Chang'e 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'e_6 "Chang'e 6")) and Earth. The satellite was announced as operational in April.
In April, NASA launched a next-generation [solar sail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sail#Advanced_Composite_Solar_Sail_System_\(ACS3\) "Solar sail") demonstration aboard a [Rocket Lab Electron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_Lab_Electron "Rocket Lab Electron").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-71)
[ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") [EarthCARE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EarthCARE "EarthCARE") launched on 28 May. Joint mission with [JAXA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA "JAXA").
NASA's [GOES-U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GOES-U "GOES-U") launched on 25 June, with the capability to detect [coronal mass ejections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronal_mass_ejection "Coronal mass ejection").
[JAXA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA "JAXA")'s [ALOS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALOS-4 "ALOS-4") launched on 1 July. It carries PALSAR-3 (Phased Array type L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar-3).
Ending the year with the launch of [PSLV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Satellite_Launch_Vehicle "Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle")C-60 on 30 December 2024, [ISRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISRO "ISRO") launched the [SpaDeX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaDeX "SpaDeX") mission, which aims to prove the organization's docking technology.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_spaceflight#cite_note-72) This technology is crucial for ISRO's upcoming [Gaganyaan Human Spaceflight Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Human_Spaceflight_Programme "Indian Human Spaceflight Programme") and the [Chandrayaan-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrayaan-4 "Chandrayaan-4") [lunar sample return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample-return_mission "Sample-return mission") project.
